implementation_notes: The classic Python form is one sentinel per worker on the queue: item = q.get(); if item is None: break, with queue.Queue's blocking get and task_done()/join() coordinating the drain. None works only while payloads cannot be None - the robust variant uses a module-level object() sentinel compared with is. Since Python 3.13 queue.Queue and asyncio.Queue also ship shutdown() (raising ShutDown/QueueShutDown once drained), which absorbs the protocol for new code; the sentinel remains the portable idiom for older interpreters and for multiprocessing queues, which have no shutdown.
pitfalls: A None sentinel collides with legitimate None payloads; use a module-level object() sentinel and compare with is.
queue.Queue has no close(): q.join() returns when the queue is drained, but the workers are still blocked in get(), so the pills must still be posted.
Only one worker receives each pill; posting fewer pills than workers leaves consumers blocked in get() forever.

asyncio.Queue is not thread-safe and queue.Queue is not asyncio-aware - the sentinel protocol must match the queue family (and asyncio pre-3.13 workers are cancelled with task.cancel(), not a sentinel).

variants.name: queue.Queue.shutdown() / asyncio.Queue.shutdown() (Python 3.13)
variants.implementation_notes: Python 3.13 gives both queue families a built-in drain-and-stop: q.shutdown() (immediate=False) lets consumers get() the remaining items, after which get() raises queue.ShutDown (asyncio: QueueShutDown), while put() raises immediately. No reserved value travels through the queue, so None and every other payload type stay legal, and one shutdown() call releases every blocked consumer. Choose it for in-process queues on 3.13+; the sentinel remains necessary for multiprocessing.Queue and older interpreters.
pitfalls: shutdown() does not exist on multiprocessing.Queue or on interpreters before 3.13; fall back to the sentinel there.
immediate=True discards the backlog (and unblocks join even when no work was done), so it is hard termination, not a graceful drain.
put() raises ShutDown after shutdown, so producers must treat that as the normal stop signal rather than a programming error.
queue.ShutDown inherits from Exception, so a broad except Exception in the worker swallows the stop signal.
